clinicalPearls: Very rare, and defined not by histological atypia alone but by the presence of craniospinal or systemic metastasis of a pituitary tumour
Most evolve from an initially invasive adenoma, often ACTH- or prolactin-secreting, that progresses over years despite treatment
It cannot be diagnosed on the primary tumour histology alone, since demonstration of discontinuous metastatic deposits is required
Metastases may be craniospinal through the cerebrospinal fluid, involving leptomeninges, brain or spinal cord, or systemic to liver, bone or lymph nodes
Presentation is with an aggressive, treatment-resistant pituitary tumour, sometimes with new neurological symptoms from metastases
Functioning carcinomas continue to secrete hormone, for example persistent hypercortisolism or hyperprolactinaemia
Management is multimodal with surgery, radiotherapy and increasingly temozolomide chemotherapy
reference.pathophysiology: Pituitary carcinoma is a malignant tumour of adenohypophyseal cells distinguished from an aggressive adenoma solely by the presence of metastasis outside the sellar region, either craniospinal spread through the cerebrospinal fluid or systemic dissemination. It typically develops through stepwise progression of an invasive, hormonally active adenoma, most commonly corticotroph or lactotroph, that accumulates further molecular alterations, increasing proliferative and invasive capacity over a prolonged latency. Continued hormone secretion by functioning tumours perpetuates the associated endocrine syndrome, while metastatic deposits cause site-specific neurological or systemic effects.
additionalDifferentials: Aggressive but non-metastatic invasive pituitary adenoma
Pituitary metastasis from another primary such as breast or lung, the reverse situation
Other malignant sellar or parasellar tumours such as germ cell tumour, chordoma or sarcoma
Lymphoma or leukaemic infiltration of the sella
additionalInvestigations: Whole-neuraxis MRI of brain and spine to detect craniospinal metastases
Systemic staging imaging with CT and functional imaging such as somatostatin-receptor PET for distant spread
Histopathology showing high proliferation indices such as elevated Ki-67, mitoses and p53 to support aggressiveness
Biopsy confirmation of a metastatic deposit to establish the diagnosis
Serial hormone measurement for functioning tumours, for example ACTH and cortisol or prolactin
Assessment of anterior and posterior pituitary function
redFlags: Rapid tumour progression or new neurological deficits despite prior treatment
Discovery of discontinuous central nervous system or systemic lesions
Escalating hormone levels refractory to therapy
Leptomeningeal symptoms such as cranial neuropathies or radiculopathy
reference.prognosis: Poor overall, with limited survival once metastasis is documented, although temozolomide and multimodal therapy can achieve responses and prolong survival in some patients.
pitfalls: Expecting histology alone to distinguish carcinoma from adenoma, when metastasis is the defining criterion
Failing to image the whole neuraxis when an aggressive pituitary tumour progresses
Overlooking a pituitary metastasis from an extracranial primary, which is more common than true pituitary carcinoma
Delaying consideration of temozolomide in progressive disease
references: European Society of Endocrinology Guideline on Aggressive Pituitary Tumours and Carcinomas
management: Temozolomide as first-line systemic chemotherapy for aggressive metastatic disease
Maximal safe surgical debulking of the primary tumour and accessible metastatic deposits
Fractionated or stereotactic radiotherapy for local control and symptomatic metastases
Control of persistent hormone excess with dopamine agonists for lactotroph tumours, and steroidogenesis inhibitors or bilateral adrenalectomy for corticotroph hypercortisolism
Replacement of resultant hypopituitarism with glucocorticoid, thyroid hormone and sex-steroid therapy
Serial whole-neuraxis MRI and tumour hormone marker surveillance to detect progression
Consider immune checkpoint inhibitors or peptide-receptor radionuclide therapy in temozolomide-refractory disease
Management within a specialist neuro-endocrine multidisciplinary team with early palliative care involvement
